lines: | Terminals survive an app install | the detached pty-daemon is what actually owns the user's shells, and it already survives a host-service restart by design — but it could never survive an APP INSTALL, because everything it executed lived in `$INSTDIR`: its process image was `Superset.exe` itself, it mapped `conpty.node` out of `resources\app.asar.unpacked`, and it inherited host-service's cwd (the spawn passed none). Any ONE of those is enough that Windows refuses to let the installer replace the file, so the installer's only remaining move is to kill the daemon — taking every live terminal with it. Before the FIRST daemon spawn on Windows the supervisor therefore materialises a self-contained runtime under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Superset\pty-runtime\<key>\`: the Electron runtime files from the install root with the binary copied under a DIFFERENT NAME (`superset-ptyd.exe` — electron-builder's one-click NSIS kills running processes by matching `${APP_EXECUTABLE_FILENAME}`, so a renamed image is not a target), `locales\`, the daemon's own `dist/main/pty-daemon.js` plus the ENTIRE hash-named `chunks/` dir (never an enumerated chunk list — that is `SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT` in another costume), and `node-pty` + `@lydell/node-pty-<platform>-<arch>` placed where ordinary Node resolution walking up from the script finds them. 364 MB, against 2.21 GB for the whole install dir, because `resources/` (the 1.2 GB asar the daemon never reads) is excluded structurally rather than by filter. The daemon is then spawned with that exe, that script and an explicit `cwd` inside the runtime, so it holds no handle anywhere in `$INSTDIR`; host-service itself stays in the install dir and still dies with the app, and the next boot re-adopts the surviving daemon over its org-hashed named pipe exactly as it already does across host-service restarts. The cache key is `<pty-daemon package version>-e<electron version>-<sha256(entry script)[:12]>`: the package version is the SAME value `EXPECTED_DAEMON_VERSION` already uses to judge a running daemon stale, so no new notion of "a different daemon" is introduced; the Electron version is in because the copied binary IS the runtime; and hashing the 42 KB ENTRY transitively covers the chunk set, since chunks are content-hash-named and referenced by name from it. An app release that does not touch the daemon reuses the existing runtime for one read plus one stat; a cold materialisation costs ~8 s and runs on the ASYNC fs API inside host-service — never on Electron's main thread, whose blocking startup fs starves the `superset-app://` loader and blanks the window for minutes. Crash-consistent by construction, because the installer can hard-kill at any moment: everything stages in `<key>.tmp-<rand>`, the copied binary is SMOKE-TESTED for real (`superset-ptyd.exe -e "require('node-pty');require('node-pty/requireBinary').requireBinary('conpty.node')"` must exit 42, which proves the file set boots AND that the native addon actually LOADS under this Electron's ABI). That second require is load-bearing, not decoration: @lydell's `WindowsPtyAgent` loads `conpty.node` LAZILY, in its constructor, so `require("node-pty")` on its own imports nothing but JS and a runtime whose prebuild is missing, quarantined or built for the wrong arch passes the test, commits `.ready`, and then fails at the first terminal the user opens. Measured on the shipped Electron against a copy of the packaged `node_modules` with `conpty.node` deleted: the JS-only script still exits 42, the addon-loading one exits 1. The load goes through node-pty's OWN platform/arch resolver, so nothing here hardcodes win32-arm64, no DLL list has to be asserted, and an Electron upgrade that adds a file cannot silently produce a dead runtime, the `.ready` marker is written INSIDE the staging dir, and the rename into place is the single atomic commit. A directory without `.ready` is not-ready and is rebuilt — and so is one WITH `.ready` whose `superset-ptyd.exe` or entry script has gone missing, because the marker is an ordinary file in an ordinary user-writable directory and the binary beside it is unsigned, freshly written and freshly RENAMED, which is an antivirus heuristic bullseye. Trusting the marker alone would make every spawn ENOENT while still reporting `reused`, opening the crash circuit and leaving the user with NO terminals at all — the one outcome this feature exists to prevent — because the loud fallback below only ever fired on a MATERIALISATION failure. Two stats on reuse close that. Reclaiming an old runtime is the one operation here that can destroy a working install, so it is gated twice: a `.refs/<pid>.json` record claims a key for a live daemon pid (a recycled pid can only ever over-protect), a runtime committed in the last five minutes is skipped outright because the daemon it was built for may not have a pid to claim it with yet, and every removal RENAMES the directory first, which Windows refuses while it is a live process's cwd or holds a mapped image — so a lost ref file degrades to "skipped, retried next spawn", never to a half-deleted live runtime whose plain-`.js` conout worker and console-list agent would be unlinked out from under it. A materialisation failure falls back to today's install-directory spawn but says so LOUDLY (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_unavailable` plus a console error naming the consequence), and so does a relocated runtime that materialises fine but cannot actually start a daemon: it is discarded (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_spawn_failed`) and the spawn is retried from the install directory in the same breath. Discarding removes the ready marker and NEVER the files — another org's daemon may be live in there, and unlinking its plain-`.js` conout worker underneath it is exactly what the rename gate exists to prevent: believing you are protected when you are not is worse than not being protected, and leaving the user with no terminals at all is worse than both. `fs.access` is deliberately NOT used to probe the sources — measured on the shipped Electron 41.10.3, `access` answers ENOENT for every DIRECTORY inside `app.asar` while `stat` and `readdir` work, so an `access`-based probe passes every real-filesystem test and then fails on every packaged install | `(PTY-RUNTIME-SIDECAR)` |

lines: | Terminals survive an app install | the detached pty-daemon is what actually owns the user's shells, and it already survives a host-service restart by design — but it could never survive an APP INSTALL, because everything it executed lived in `$INSTDIR`: its process image was `Superset.exe` itself, it mapped `conpty.node` out of `resources\app.asar.unpacked`, and it inherited host-service's cwd (the spawn passed none). Any ONE of those is enough that Windows refuses to let the installer replace the file, so the installer's only remaining move is to kill the daemon — taking every live terminal with it. Before the FIRST daemon spawn on Windows the supervisor therefore materialises a self-contained runtime under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Superset\pty-runtime\<key>\`: the Electron runtime files from the install root with the binary copied under a DIFFERENT NAME (`superset-ptyd.exe` — electron-builder's one-click NSIS kills running processes by matching `${APP_EXECUTABLE_FILENAME}`, so a renamed image is not a target), `locales\`, the daemon's own `dist/main/pty-daemon.js` plus the ENTIRE hash-named `chunks/` dir (never an enumerated chunk list — that is `SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT` in another costume), and `node-pty` + `@lydell/node-pty-<platform>-<arch>` placed where ordinary Node resolution walking up from the script finds them. 364 MB, against 2.21 GB for the whole install dir, because `resources/` (the 1.2 GB asar the daemon never reads) is excluded structurally rather than by filter. The daemon is then spawned with that exe, that script and an explicit `cwd` inside the runtime, so it holds no handle anywhere in `$INSTDIR`; host-service itself stays in the install dir and still dies with the app, and the next boot re-adopts the surviving daemon over its org-hashed named pipe exactly as it already does across host-service restarts. The cache key is `<pty-daemon package version>-e<electron version>-<sha256(entry script)[:12]>`: the package version is the SAME value `EXPECTED_DAEMON_VERSION` already uses to judge a running daemon stale, so no new notion of "a different daemon" is introduced; the Electron version is in because the copied binary IS the runtime; and hashing the 42 KB ENTRY transitively covers the chunk set, since chunks are content-hash-named and referenced by name from it. An app release that does not touch the daemon reuses the existing runtime for one read plus one stat; a cold materialisation costs ~8 s and runs on the ASYNC fs API inside host-service — never on Electron's main thread, whose blocking startup fs starves the `superset-app://` loader and blanks the window for minutes. Crash-consistent by construction, because the installer can hard-kill at any moment: everything stages in `<key>.tmp-<rand>`, the copied binary is SMOKE-TESTED for real (`superset-ptyd.exe -e "require('node-pty');require('node-pty/requireBinary').requireBinary('conpty.node')"` must exit 42, which proves the file set boots AND that the native addon actually LOADS under this Electron's ABI). That second require is load-bearing, not decoration: @lydell's `WindowsPtyAgent` loads `conpty.node` LAZILY, in its constructor, so `require("node-pty")` on its own imports nothing but JS and a runtime whose prebuild is missing, quarantined or built for the wrong arch passes the test, commits `.ready`, and then fails at the first terminal the user opens. Measured on the shipped Electron against a copy of the packaged `node_modules` with `conpty.node` deleted: the JS-only script still exits 42, the addon-loading one exits 1. The load goes through node-pty's OWN platform/arch resolver, so nothing here hardcodes win32-arm64, no DLL list has to be asserted, and an Electron upgrade that adds a file cannot silently produce a dead runtime, the `.ready` marker is written INSIDE the staging dir, and the rename into place is the single atomic commit. A directory without `.ready` is not-ready and is rebuilt — and so is one WITH `.ready` whose `superset-ptyd.exe` or entry script has gone missing, because the marker is an ordinary file in an ordinary user-writable directory and the binary beside it is unsigned, freshly written and freshly RENAMED, which is an antivirus heuristic bullseye. Trusting the marker alone would make every spawn ENOENT while still reporting `reused`, opening the crash circuit and leaving the user with NO terminals at all — the one outcome this feature exists to prevent — because the loud fallback below only ever fired on a MATERIALISATION failure. Two stats on reuse close that. Reclaiming an old runtime is the one operation here that can destroy a working install, so it is gated twice: a `.refs/<pid>.json` record claims a key for a live daemon pid (a recycled pid can only ever over-protect), a runtime committed in the last five minutes is skipped outright because the daemon it was built for may not have a pid to claim it with yet, and every removal RENAMES the directory first, which Windows refuses while it is a live process's cwd or holds a mapped image — so a lost ref file degrades to "skipped, retried next spawn", never to a half-deleted live runtime whose plain-`.js` conout worker and console-list agent would be unlinked out from under it. A materialisation failure falls back to today's install-directory spawn but says so LOUDLY (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_unavailable` plus a console error naming the consequence), and so does a relocated runtime that materialises fine but cannot actually start a daemon: it is discarded (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_spawn_failed`) and the spawn is retried from the install directory in the same breath. Discarding removes the ready marker and NEVER the files — another org's daemon may be live in there, and unlinking its plain-`.js` conout worker underneath it is exactly what the rename gate exists to prevent: believing you are protected when you are not is worse than not being protected, and leaving the user with no terminals at all is worse than both. `fs.access` is deliberately NOT used to probe the sources — measured on the shipped Electron 41.10.3, `access` answers ENOENT for every DIRECTORY inside `app.asar` while `stat` and `readdir` work, so an `access`-based probe passes every real-filesystem test and then fails on every packaged install | `(PTY-RUNTIME-SIDECAR)` |

lines: | Terminals survive an app install | the detached pty-daemon is what actually owns the user's shells, and it already survives a host-service restart by design — but it could never survive an APP INSTALL, because everything it executed lived in `$INSTDIR`: its process image was `Superset.exe` itself, it mapped `conpty.node` out of `resources\app.asar.unpacked`, and it inherited host-service's cwd (the spawn passed none). Any ONE of those is enough that Windows refuses to let the installer replace the file, so the installer's only remaining move is to kill the daemon — taking every live terminal with it. Before the FIRST daemon spawn on Windows the supervisor therefore materialises a self-contained runtime under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Superset\pty-runtime\<key>\`: the Electron runtime files from the install root with the binary copied under a DIFFERENT NAME (`superset-ptyd.exe` — electron-builder's one-click NSIS kills running processes by matching `${APP_EXECUTABLE_FILENAME}`, so a renamed image is not a target), `locales\`, the daemon's own `dist/main/pty-daemon.js` plus the ENTIRE hash-named `chunks/` dir (never an enumerated chunk list — that is `SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT` in another costume), and `node-pty` + `@lydell/node-pty-<platform>-<arch>` placed where ordinary Node resolution walking up from the script finds them. 364 MB, against 2.21 GB for the whole install dir, because `resources/` (the 1.2 GB asar the daemon never reads) is excluded structurally rather than by filter. The daemon is then spawned with that exe, that script and an explicit `cwd` inside the runtime, so it holds no handle anywhere in `$INSTDIR`; host-service itself stays in the install dir and still dies with the app, and the next boot re-adopts the surviving daemon over its org-hashed named pipe exactly as it already does across host-service restarts. The cache key is `<pty-daemon package version>-e<electron version>-<sha256(entry script)[:12]>`: the package version is the SAME value `EXPECTED_DAEMON_VERSION` already uses to judge a running daemon stale, so no new notion of "a different daemon" is introduced; the Electron version is in because the copied binary IS the runtime; and hashing the 42 KB ENTRY transitively covers the chunk set, since chunks are content-hash-named and referenced by name from it. An app release that does not touch the daemon reuses the existing runtime for one read plus one stat; a cold materialisation costs ~8 s and runs on the ASYNC fs API inside host-service — never on Electron's main thread, whose blocking startup fs starves the `superset-app://` loader and blanks the window for minutes. Crash-consistent by construction, because the installer can hard-kill at any moment: everything stages in `<key>.tmp-<rand>`, the copied binary is SMOKE-TESTED for real (`superset-ptyd.exe -e "require('node-pty');require('node-pty/requireBinary').requireBinary('conpty.node')"` must exit 42, which proves the file set boots AND that the native addon actually LOADS under this Electron's ABI). That second require is load-bearing, not decoration: @lydell's `WindowsPtyAgent` loads `conpty.node` LAZILY, in its constructor, so `require("node-pty")` on its own imports nothing but JS and a runtime whose prebuild is missing, quarantined or built for the wrong arch passes the test, commits `.ready`, and then fails at the first terminal the user opens. Measured on the shipped Electron against a copy of the packaged `node_modules` with `conpty.node` deleted: the JS-only script still exits 42, the addon-loading one exits 1. The load goes through node-pty's OWN platform/arch resolver, so nothing here hardcodes win32-arm64, no DLL list has to be asserted, and an Electron upgrade that adds a file cannot silently produce a dead runtime, the `.ready` marker is written INSIDE the staging dir, and the rename into place is the single atomic commit. A directory without `.ready` is not-ready and is rebuilt — and so is one WITH `.ready` whose `superset-ptyd.exe` or entry script has gone missing, because the marker is an ordinary file in an ordinary user-writable directory and the binary beside it is unsigned, freshly written and freshly RENAMED, which is an antivirus heuristic bullseye. Trusting the marker alone would make every spawn ENOENT while still reporting `reused`, opening the crash circuit and leaving the user with NO terminals at all — the one outcome this feature exists to prevent — because the loud fallback below only ever fired on a MATERIALISATION failure. Two stats on reuse close that. Reclaiming an old runtime is the one operation here that can destroy a working install, so it is gated twice: a `.refs/<pid>.json` record claims a key for a live daemon pid (a recycled pid can only ever over-protect), a runtime committed in the last five minutes is skipped outright because the daemon it was built for may not have a pid to claim it with yet, and every removal RENAMES the directory first, which Windows refuses while it is a live process's cwd or holds a mapped image — so a lost ref file degrades to "skipped, retried next spawn", never to a half-deleted live runtime whose plain-`.js` conout worker and console-list agent would be unlinked out from under it. A materialisation failure falls back to today's install-directory spawn but says so LOUDLY (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_unavailable` plus a console error naming the consequence), and so does a relocated runtime that materialises fine but cannot actually start a daemon: it is discarded (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_spawn_failed`) and the spawn is retried from the install directory in the same breath. Discarding removes the ready marker and NEVER the files — another org's daemon may be live in there, and unlinking its plain-`.js` conout worker underneath it is exactly what the rename gate exists to prevent: believing you are protected when you are not is worse than not being protected, and leaving the user with no terminals at all is worse than both. `fs.access` is deliberately NOT used to probe the sources — measured on the shipped Electron 41.10.3, `access` answers ENOENT for every DIRECTORY inside `app.asar` while `stat` and `readdir` work, so an `access`-based probe passes every real-filesystem test and then fails on every packaged install | `(PTY-RUNTIME-SIDECAR)` |

lines: | Terminals survive an app install | the detached pty-daemon is what actually owns the user's shells, and it already survives a host-service restart by design — but it could never survive an APP INSTALL, because everything it executed lived in `$INSTDIR`: its process image was `Superset.exe` itself, it mapped `conpty.node` out of `resources\app.asar.unpacked`, and it inherited host-service's cwd (the spawn passed none). Any ONE of those is enough that Windows refuses to let the installer replace the file, so the installer's only remaining move is to kill the daemon — taking every live terminal with it. Before the FIRST daemon spawn on Windows the supervisor therefore materialises a self-contained runtime under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Superset\pty-runtime\<key>\`: the Electron runtime files from the install root with the binary copied under a DIFFERENT NAME (`superset-ptyd.exe` — electron-builder's one-click NSIS kills running processes by matching `${APP_EXECUTABLE_FILENAME}`, so a renamed image is not a target), `locales\`, the daemon's own `dist/main/pty-daemon.js` plus the ENTIRE hash-named `chunks/` dir (never an enumerated chunk list — that is `SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT` in another costume), and `node-pty` + `@lydell/node-pty-<platform>-<arch>` placed where ordinary Node resolution walking up from the script finds them. 364 MB, against 2.21 GB for the whole install dir, because `resources/` (the 1.2 GB asar the daemon never reads) is excluded structurally rather than by filter. The daemon is then spawned with that exe, that script and an explicit `cwd` inside the runtime, so it holds no handle anywhere in `$INSTDIR`; host-service itself stays in the install dir and still dies with the app, and the next boot re-adopts the surviving daemon over its org-hashed named pipe exactly as it already does across host-service restarts. The cache key is `<pty-daemon package version>-e<electron version>-<sha256(entry script)[:12]>`: the package version is the SAME value `EXPECTED_DAEMON_VERSION` already uses to judge a running daemon stale, so no new notion of "a different daemon" is introduced; the Electron version is in because the copied binary IS the runtime; and hashing the 42 KB ENTRY transitively covers the chunk set, since chunks are content-hash-named and referenced by name from it. An app release that does not touch the daemon reuses the existing runtime for one read plus one stat; a cold materialisation costs ~8 s and runs on the ASYNC fs API inside host-service — never on Electron's main thread, whose blocking startup fs starves the `superset-app://` loader and blanks the window for minutes. Crash-consistent by construction, because the installer can hard-kill at any moment: everything stages in `<key>.tmp-<rand>`, the copied binary is SMOKE-TESTED for real (`superset-ptyd.exe -e "require('node-pty');require('node-pty/requireBinary').requireBinary('conpty.node')"` must exit 42, which proves the file set boots AND that the native addon actually LOADS under this Electron's ABI). That second require is load-bearing, not decoration: @lydell's `WindowsPtyAgent` loads `conpty.node` LAZILY, in its constructor, so `require("node-pty")` on its own imports nothing but JS and a runtime whose prebuild is missing, quarantined or built for the wrong arch passes the test, commits `.ready`, and then fails at the first terminal the user opens. Measured on the shipped Electron against a copy of the packaged `node_modules` with `conpty.node` deleted: the JS-only script still exits 42, the addon-loading one exits 1. The load goes through node-pty's OWN platform/arch resolver, so nothing here hardcodes win32-arm64, no DLL list has to be asserted, and an Electron upgrade that adds a file cannot silently produce a dead runtime, the `.ready` marker is written INSIDE the staging dir, and the rename into place is the single atomic commit. A directory without `.ready` is not-ready and is rebuilt — and so is one WITH `.ready` whose `superset-ptyd.exe` or entry script has gone missing, because the marker is an ordinary file in an ordinary user-writable directory and the binary beside it is unsigned, freshly written and freshly RENAMED, which is an antivirus heuristic bullseye. Trusting the marker alone would make every spawn ENOENT while still reporting `reused`, opening the crash circuit and leaving the user with NO terminals at all — the one outcome this feature exists to prevent — because the loud fallback below only ever fired on a MATERIALISATION failure. Two stats on reuse close that. Reclaiming an old runtime is the one operation here that can destroy a working install, so it is gated twice: a `.refs/<pid>.json` record claims a key for a live daemon pid (a recycled pid can only ever over-protect), a runtime committed in the last five minutes is skipped outright because the daemon it was built for may not have a pid to claim it with yet, and every removal RENAMES the directory first, which Windows refuses while it is a live process's cwd or holds a mapped image — so a lost ref file degrades to "skipped, retried next spawn", never to a half-deleted live runtime whose plain-`.js` conout worker and console-list agent would be unlinked out from under it. A materialisation failure falls back to today's install-directory spawn but says so LOUDLY (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_unavailable` plus a console error naming the consequence), and so does a relocated runtime that materialises fine but cannot actually start a daemon: it is discarded (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_spawn_failed`) and the spawn is retried from the install directory in the same breath. Discarding removes the ready marker and NEVER the files — another org's daemon may be live in there, and unlinking its plain-`.js` conout worker underneath it is exactly what the rename gate exists to prevent: believing you are protected when you are not is worse than not being protected, and leaving the user with no terminals at all is worse than both. `fs.access` is deliberately NOT used to probe the sources — measured on the shipped Electron 41.10.3, `access` answers ENOENT for every DIRECTORY inside `app.asar` while `stat` and `readdir` work, so an `access`-based probe passes every real-filesystem test and then fails on every packaged install | `(PTY-RUNTIME-SIDECAR)` |

| Hook endpoint healing | the embedded Python status hook fails over to every `~/.superset/host/*/manifest.json` endpoint (org-first, positive `ignored:false` acceptance, 4 s probe budget) when the env-frozen host URL is dead, so a host-service port change can no longer strand a terminal's status events - including the red-dot-clearing answer signal; manifests of dead host processes are skipped via a pid liveness probe `(HOOK-STALE-MANIFEST)`; the hook debug log now rotates at 1 MB | `(HOOK-ENDPOINT-HEAL)` |

| Manual status dismissal | right-click Clear Status is authoritative: a host-side mutation deletes the terminal's `.askq` question markers behind an mtime fence (a question raised after the click survives), forces bindings to `Stop`, retracts companion questions via `markStale` + a `question.stale` frame, and the renderer then clears every latched axis and stamps the seen watermark so no resync resurrects the dot | `(MANUAL-DISMISS)` |

lines: | Terminals survive an app install | the detached pty-daemon is what actually owns the user's shells, and it already survives a host-service restart by design — but it could never survive an APP INSTALL, because everything it executed lived in `$INSTDIR`: its process image was `Superset.exe` itself, it mapped `conpty.node` out of `resources\app.asar.unpacked`, and it inherited host-service's cwd (the spawn passed none). Any ONE of those is enough that Windows refuses to let the installer replace the file, so the installer's only remaining move is to kill the daemon — taking every live terminal with it. Before the FIRST daemon spawn on Windows the supervisor therefore materialises a self-contained runtime under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Superset\pty-runtime\<key>\`: the Electron runtime files from the install root with the binary copied under a DIFFERENT NAME (`superset-ptyd.exe` — electron-builder's one-click NSIS kills running processes by matching `${APP_EXECUTABLE_FILENAME}`, so a renamed image is not a target), `locales\`, the daemon's own `dist/main/pty-daemon.js` plus the ENTIRE hash-named `chunks/` dir (never an enumerated chunk list — that is `SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT` in another costume), and `node-pty` + `@lydell/node-pty-<platform>-<arch>` placed where ordinary Node resolution walking up from the script finds them. 364 MB, against 2.21 GB for the whole install dir, because `resources/` (the 1.2 GB asar the daemon never reads) is excluded structurally rather than by filter. lines: | Terminals survive an app install | the detached pty-daemon is what actually owns the user's shells, and it already survives a host-service restart by design — but it could never survive an APP INSTALL, because everything it executed lived in `$INSTDIR`: its process image was `Superset.exe` itself, it mapped `conpty.node` out of `resources\app.asar.unpacked`, and it inherited host-service's cwd (the spawn passed none). Any ONE of those is enough that Windows refuses to let the installer replace the file, so the installer's only remaining move is to kill the daemon — taking every live terminal with it. Before the FIRST daemon spawn on Windows the supervisor therefore materialises a self-contained runtime under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Superset\pty-runtime\<key>\`: the Electron runtime files from the install root with the binary copied under a DIFFERENT NAME (`superset-ptyd.exe` — electron-builder's one-click NSIS kills running processes by matching `${APP_EXECUTABLE_FILENAME}`, so a renamed image is not a target), `locales\`, the daemon's own `dist/main/pty-daemon.js` plus the ENTIRE hash-named `chunks/` dir (never an enumerated chunk list — that is `SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT` in another costume), and `node-pty` + `@lydell/node-pty-<platform>-<arch>` placed where ordinary Node resolution walking up from the script finds them. 364 MB, against 2.21 GB for the whole install dir, because `resources/` (the 1.2 GB asar the daemon never reads) is excluded structurally rather than by filter. The daemon is then spawned with that exe, that script and an explicit `cwd` inside the runtime, so it holds no handle anywhere in `$INSTDIR`; host-service itself stays in the install dir and still dies with the app, and the next boot re-adopts the surviving daemon over its org-hashed named pipe exactly as it already does across host-service restarts. The cache key is `<pty-daemon package version>-e<electron version>-<sha256(entry script)[:12]>`: the package version is the SAME value `EXPECTED_DAEMON_VERSION` already uses to judge a running daemon stale, so no new notion of "a different daemon" is introduced; the Electron version is in because the copied binary IS the runtime; and hashing the 42 KB ENTRY transitively covers the chunk set, since chunks are content-hash-named and referenced by name from it. An app release that does not touch the daemon reuses the existing runtime for one read plus one stat; a cold materialisation costs ~8 s and runs on the ASYNC fs API inside host-service — never on Electron's main thread, whose blocking startup fs starves the `superset-app://` loader and blanks the window for minutes. Crash-consistent by construction, because the installer can hard-kill at any moment: everything stages in `<key>.tmp-<rand>`, the copied binary is SMOKE-TESTED for real (`superset-ptyd.exe -e "require('node-pty');require('node-pty/requireBinary').requireBinary('conpty.node')"` must exit 42, which proves the file set boots AND that the native addon actually LOADS under this Electron's ABI). That second require is load-bearing, not decoration: @lydell's `WindowsPtyAgent` loads `conpty.node` LAZILY, in its constructor, so `require("node-pty")` on its own imports nothing but JS and a runtime whose prebuild is missing, quarantined or built for the wrong arch passes the test, commits `.ready`, and then fails at the first terminal the user opens. Measured on the shipped Electron against a copy of the packaged `node_modules` with `conpty.node` deleted: the JS-only script still exits 42, the addon-loading one exits 1. The load goes through node-pty's OWN platform/arch resolver, so nothing here hardcodes win32-arm64, no DLL list has to be asserted, and an Electron upgrade that adds a file cannot silently produce a dead runtime, the `.ready` marker is written INSIDE the staging dir, and the rename into place is the single atomic commit. A directory without `.ready` is not-ready and is rebuilt — and so is one WITH `.ready` whose `superset-ptyd.exe` or entry script has gone missing, because the marker is an ordinary file in an ordinary user-writable directory and the binary beside it is unsigned, freshly written and freshly RENAMED, which is an antivirus heuristic bullseye. Trusting the marker alone would make every spawn ENOENT while still reporting `reused`, opening the crash circuit and leaving the user with NO terminals at all — the one outcome this feature exists to prevent — because the loud fallback below only ever fired on a MATERIALISATION failure. Two stats on reuse close that. Reclaiming an old runtime is the one operation here that can destroy a working install, so it is gated twice: a `.refs/<pid>.json` record claims a key for a live daemon pid (a recycled pid can only ever over-protect), a runtime committed in the last five minutes is skipped outright because the daemon it was built for may not have a pid to claim it with yet, and every removal RENAMES the directory first, which Windows refuses while it is a live process's cwd or holds a mapped image — so a lost ref file degrades to "skipped, retried next spawn", never to a half-deleted live runtime whose plain-`.js` conout worker and console-list agent would be unlinked out from under it. A materialisation failure falls back to today's install-directory spawn but says so LOUDLY (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_unavailable` plus a console error naming the consequence), and so does a relocated runtime that materialises fine but cannot actually start a daemon: it is discarded (`pty_daemon_runtime_sidecar_spawn_failed`) and the spawn is retried from the install directory in the same breath. Discarding removes the ready marker and NEVER the files — another org's daemon may be live in there, and unlinking its plain-`.js` conout worker underneath it is exactly what the rename gate exists to prevent: believing you are protected when you are not is worse than not being protected, and leaving the user with no terminals at all is worse than both. `fs.access` is deliberately NOT used to probe the sources — measured on the shipped Electron 41.10.3, `access` answers ENOENT for every DIRECTORY inside `app.asar` while `stat` and `readdir` work, so an `access`-based probe passes every real-filesystem test and then fails on every packaged install | `(PTY-RUNTIME-SIDECAR)` |

| Hook endpoint healing | the embedded Python status hook fails over to every `~/.superset/host/*/manifest.json` endpoint (org-first, positive `ignored:false` acceptance, 4 s probe budget) when the env-frozen host URL is dead, so a host-service port change can no longer strand a terminal's status events - including the red-dot-clearing answer signal; manifests of dead host processes are skipped via a pid liveness probe `(HOOK-STALE-MANIFEST)`; the hook debug log now rotates at 1 MB | `(HOOK-ENDPOINT-HEAL)` |

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

def _decide_event_type(
    event,
    tool,
    terminal_id,
    sub_agent_id,
    has_background,
    has_agent_background,
    has_shell_background,
    bg_ids,
    trigger,
    source,
    session_id,
    reason_out=None,
):
    # (UNTAGGED-BG-RED) CENTRAL RED GUARD. The renderer has ONE permission axis per
    # terminal, so a red-CLEARING result (Start, or a green/blue turn-end) must NEVER
    # be emitted while a question owner is still live in the .askq dir — that would
    # clear a co-pending question's red. EVERY decision funnels through here, so no
    # individual branch (answer, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, the compact
    # paths, ...) can drop the red. When a held result is a turn-end
    # (Stop/BackgroundRunning), mark .mainstopped so the eventual last SubagentStop
    # still finalizes to green once the dir empties. (The inner branches already
    # _remove the answered/own owner and _reap_askq dead owners first, so the count
    # here is the set of GENUINELY still-open questions.)
    askq_dir = _askq_dir(terminal_id)
    before = _running_count(askq_dir)
    result = _decide_event_type_inner(
        event, tool, terminal_id, sub_agent_id, has_background,
        has_agent_background, has_shell_background, bg_ids, trigger, source,
        session_id, reason_out,
    )
    after = _running_count(askq_dir)
    # DOWNGRADE: never clear a red while a question owner is still live -> hold
    # SubagentActive (stamp .mainstopped on a held turn-end so the last SubagentStop
    # can still finalize green once the dir empties).
    if result in ("Start", "Stop", "BackgroundRunning") and after > 0:
        if result != "Start":
            _touch(_sentinel_path(terminal_id))
        return "SubagentActive"
    # UPGRADE: this event removed the LAST question owner (answered / cancelled
    # SubagentStop / reaped) but the inner returned a NON-clearing result
    # (SubagentActive for a yellow/agent/codex hold, or None for a no-op) — so the
    # now-stale permission red would latch. Emit Start to clear it; working still
    # shows (red>working only applied while an owner existed), and the next genuine
    # turn-end greens. Without this, a cancelled subagent question or a main Stop
    # held by other subagents would leave the answered/gone question's red stuck.
    if (
        event != "SessionStart"  # a fresh-session cleanup empties the dir but resolves NO question -> never assert working
        and before > 0
        and after == 0
        and (result is None or result == "SubagentActive")
    ):
        return "Start"
    return result

/**
 * (ONE-BUZZ-UNTIL-READ) The instant a lifecycle event happened, forced to be
 * STRICTLY INCREASING per terminal.
 *
 * `Date.now()` is not monotonic: an NTP correction can step the wall clock
 * BACKWARDS, and every lifecycle fact this host records is stamped from it —
 * the binding's `lastEventAt`, the deterministic alert id, the `gx` generation
 * on `g` and `c`, and the boundary `markLifecycleSeen` compares a read
 * against. A backstep therefore does not merely mis-date a row, it INVERTS an
 * ordering three separate mechanisms trust:
 *
 *  - the phone shows the newer generation and drops the older, so a finish
 *    stamped behind its predecessor is rejected as stale and never buzzes;
 *  - a later `c` computed from the read cannot name the card that IS showing,
 *    so the notification cannot be retracted at all;
 *  - the renderer sees the report accepted and drops its outstanding record,
 *    which is the evidence the resync repair would have used.
 *
 * The anchor is the terminal's own last event, which is persisted with the
 * binding and reloaded on start, so the property survives a host restart
 * without a schema change — the same state the deterministic-id path already
 * depends on. Per terminal rather than global: two terminals' streams are
 * independent, and one busy agent must not push another's stamps into the
 * future.
 *
 * Forward jumps are honoured as-is. Only the backstep is corrected, by the
 * smallest amount that keeps the order intact.
 *
 * Lives in a leaf module so BOTH producers of lifecycle events — the
 * notifications hook route and the (STALE-WORKING-SWEEP) — share one copy of
 * the ordering rule.
 */
export function nextLifecycleInstantMs(
	nowMs: number,
	previousEventAtMs: number | null | undefined,
): number {
	if (previousEventAtMs === null || previousEventAtMs === undefined) {
		return nowMs;
	}
	return nowMs > previousEventAtMs ? nowMs : previousEventAtMs + 1;
}

Done. All /simplify findings applied, everything green. Final state:

## Root cause (all four confirmed in your logs)

Your eMAR terminal's actual death: the final Stop held yellow for teammate rows and **deleted the `.mainstopped` sentinel while doing it**, so the last `SubagentStop` at 19:56 — carrying only one zombie row, with teammate activity 54 minutes stale — hit a silent no-op path instead of the decision that would have greened it. Behind that sat three more defects: teammates stopped via Stop Task latch `active` forever in the ledger; row-trust never bound a single row all day (`trustedEntryIds: []` in both sessions); and nothing ever re-evaluates after the last hook event, so all the existing staleness reaps were unreachable.

## The permafix (4 layers)

1. **Sentinel policy centralized** in the decision wrapper: hold results at a turn-end keep `.mainstopped`, true turn-ends consume it — enforced once, so no future branch can repeat the per-site mistake. The silent no-op path now writes a `NOOP:` line to dot-decisions.log.
2. **TaskStop pairing**: a teammate is marked idle when its TaskStop's non-error tool result confirms the stop.
3. **Spawn-credit trust** (cache v7): per-description name-set + 15-minute wall-clock credit slots replace the never-satisfiable same-delta rule; misses log `spawn-credit-miss`.
4. **Host-service stale-working sweep** — the guarantee: every 5 minutes it finalizes any working dot with no events for 30 minutes, a recorded turn end, and every hook-owned hold cold at its own window (12h run markers, 2h compaction, codex jobs honored, reds never touched). It moves the dot silently (no late chime/toast), notifies your phone/watch, and logs `STALE-SWEEP` into the same audit file.

All three reviewers' findings (Sol 6, Fable 6, Opus 9) were fixed or already covered; two accepted residuals are documented in FEATURES.md (a same-text workflow row created inside the 15-minute credit window can still bind, and the codex-probe logic now exists in three runtimes — consolidation debt, noted). Verified: 91 desktop watcher/hook tests, 94 host-service tests, both typechecks, marker gate 265/265.

The two currently-stuck dots clear on your next message in those chats (or right-click → Clear Status). Everything is uncommitted on `main`, ready for you to review and commit — say the word and I'll commit it.
